title: Coordinate classification of reduced crystallographic rational root planes
statement:
Let $V$ be a two-dimensional vector space over the field $\mathbf Q$ [def-weil-field], [def-weil-vector-space-dimension]. Let $S\subset V\setminus\{0\}$ be finite and spanning. For every $r\in S$ suppose given a rational linear functional $c_r:V\to\mathbf Q$ such that $c_r(r)=2$, $c_r(S)\subseteq\mathbf Z$, and $s_r(x)=x-c_r(x)r$ permutes $S$. Assume reducedness: $S\cap\mathbf Qr=\{r,-r\}$ for every $r\in S$. Then there is an ordered rational basis $(s,t)$ of $V$, with $s,t\in S$, in which $S$ is exactly one of the following four sets:
$$
\begin{aligned}
A_1\times A_1 &: \{\pm s,\pm t\},\\
A_2 &: \{\pm s,\pm t,\pm(s+t)\},\\
B_2 &: \{\pm s,\pm t,\pm(s+t),\pm(2s+t)\},\\
G_2 &: \{\pm s,\pm t,\pm(s+t),\pm(2s+t),\pm(3s+t),\pm(3s+2t)\}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Each $\pm w$ denotes the two vectors $w,-w$.

source.place: Appendix C.12, C.14, C.17--C.18 (printed pp.610--611) for rational reduced crystallographic root systems; Appendix C section g, table (180) and the four rank-two diagrams (printed pp.621--622) for the classification. Rational coordinates are those in the displayed simple-root bases.

proof.text: Each $s_r$ is an involution since $c_r(r)=2$. Let $W$ be the group of linear maps generated by them. Its action on $S$ is faithful: an element fixing every vector of the spanning set fixes $V$. Thus $W$ embeds in the finite permutation group of $S$. Choose any rational basis and its sum-of-coordinate-products form $B_0$. Put $B(x,y)=\sum_{w\in W}B_0(wx,wy)$. This is rational, symmetric and positive definite, since every term $B_0(wx,wx)$ is nonnegative and the identity term is positive for $x\ne0$. Right multiplication permutes $W$, so $B(s_rx,s_ry)=B(x,y)$. Pairing $s_rx=x-c_r(x)r$ with $s_rr=-r$ gives $c_r(x)=2B(x,r)/B(r,r)$.

Apply the rational simple-base/orbit lemma to the given finite spanning set and its given functionals; reducedness and integrality are precisely its hypotheses. Obtain a basis $D\subset S$ with same-sign integral root coordinates and every root in a simple-reflection orbit. Since $\dim V=2$, write $D=\{s,t\}$, initially in either order.

Set $a=c_s(t)$ and $b=c_t(s)$, integers. The form identity gives $ab=4B(s,t)^2/(B(s,s)B(t,t))\in[0,4)$: strictness follows by evaluating positivity at $t-B(s,t)s/B(s,s)$, which is nonzero since $s,t$ are independent. Both integers have the sign of $B(s,t)$, and one is zero exactly when both are. If positive, their product is 1, 2 or 3, so one is 1. If $a=1$, the root $s_s(t)=t-s$ has mixed-sign $D$-coordinates, a contradiction; if $b=1$ use $s_t(s)=s-t$. Hence both are nonpositive. After interchanging $s,t$ their pair is $(0,0)$ or $(-m,-1)$ with $m=1,2,3$.

source.place: Appendix C section g, table (180) and the simple-root sign argument, printed p.621
Appendix C section g, four diagrams and reflection table, printed p.622; explicit coordinate substitutions

proof.text: Conversely all listed vectors occur in the union of the unit-vector orbits. The unit vectors occur by empty words. For $m=1$, $(1,1)=T(1,0)$. For $m=2$ also $(1,1)=T(1,0)$ and $(2,1)=U(0,1)$. For $m=3$, successively $(1,1)=T(1,0)$, $(2,1)=U(1,1)$, $(3,1)=U(0,1)$, $(3,2)=T(3,1)$. Negatives also occur because $U(1,0)=-(1,0)$, $T(0,1)=-(0,1)$, and linear words commute with negation. The cited lemma says that every root is such a word applied to $s$ or $t$; the reverse inclusion holds because these two roots lie in $S$ and every generator permutes $S$. Hence $S$ equals the computed orbit union. Translating each $(x,y)$ to $xs+yt$ gives exactly the four displayed sets, with $s,t\in S$ a rational basis.
